utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-95-11-A, the Prosecutor versus Milan Martic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Martic, can you hear and follow the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me call for appearances. For the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Michelle Jarvis appearing for the Prosecution; and my co-counsel today, Mr. Paul Rogers; Ms. Laurel Baig; Ms. Najwa Nabti; and our case manager again today, Ms. Lourdes Galicia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I'm Milan Martic's Defence counsel, attorney-at-law Predrag Milovancevic; and with me is my colleague, co-counsel, Nikola Perovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we hear today the appeal in the case of Prosecutor versus Milan Martic. Yesterday, the Appeals Chamber heard Martic's appeal. This morning, we'll hear the Prosecution's appeal. The Prosecution will present its submissions for one hour. Counsel for Martic will then present its response for 45 minutes, after which the Prosecution will reply for 15 minutes. At the end of the hearing, Mr. Martic will be given the opportunity, should he wish to do so, to give a ten-minutes' personal statement, and then the Appeals Chamber will adjourn. Now I would like to invite the Prosecution to present submissions in support of its appeal. Please, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and Your Honours. The Prosecution has appealed the Trial Chamber's legal error in excluding hors de combat victims from the scope of Mr. Martic's crimes against humanity convictions in this case. I will address Your Honours this morning on the two legal arguments in support of this ground of appeal, and my colleague Ms. Nabti will follow with a discussion of the application of the correct legal principles to the facts of this case and the remedy that we are seeking. As I've mentioned, I'm going to cover the two legal arguments in support of our ground of appeal, and first I'll address Your Honours on our argument that individual victims of crimes against humanity need not be civilians as long as they are targeted as part of a widespread and systematic attack against civilians. And I'll call this our chapeau argument for ease of reference throughout my submissions today. And in particular, in this part of our submissions I'll address Your Honours' question number 1 in the Scheduling Order for the preparation for this hearing. Second, I'll address our argument that in the context of Article 5 the term "civilian" encompasses persons hors de combat because they are not participants in the hostilities and are probably regarded as non-combatants in that sense of the word. I'll call this our civilian definition argument, again for ease of reference, throughout my submissions today. At this juncture I would like to make one clarification which arises out of Your Honours question number 1, and that is that you've indicated that these two positions are alternative arguments, and certainly in our appeal brief we also employed that term. And it's accurate in the sense that if Your Honours were to accept either one of these positions, the Prosecution's appeal in this case could succeed. But I would like to emphasize that the two arguments are more properly regarded as mutually reinforcing arguments, and we ask Your Honours to find both that the individual victims of crimes against humanity need not be civilians and that persons hors de combat are civilians for Article 5 purposes. Before I move on to look in more detail at each of these two legal arguments, I want to take a few moments to just emphasize the key concern underlying this ground of appeal and why we've brought this matter to the attention of Your Honours. As we've explained in our appeal brief and our reply brief, by 1991 when the crimes in this case commenced, the crimes against humanity doctrine had moved far beyond its origins in the Nuremberg charter. It had developed into a broad-based human rights protection with the objective of protecting humanity dignity in all circumstances, whether in peacetime or during war. So the crimes against humanity doctrine by this time was no longer intended merely as a vehicle to supplement war crimes provisions, to cover that conduct which would not otherwise be caught within the reach of war crimes provisions; but rather, it had become a specialised vehicle for expressing the international community's condemnation of crimes that were so widespread or systematic that the international community as a whole was affected and not just the individual victim. And it's against that background that I ask you to view Article 5 of our Statute. Article 5 is, of course, one of the key avenues in our Statute for responding to the ethnic cleansing that took place in the former Yugoslavia, the practice that had so shocked the international community and had led in large part to the establishment of this Tribunal. And the present case, of course, is a prime example of such an ethnic cleansing campaign. It would frustrate the object and purpose of Article 5 to artificially extract from the victim group people who were targeted as part of a single over-arching ethnic cleansing campaign simply because they happened to be members of the armed forces. In fact, due to the system of territorial defence employed in the former Yugoslavia, such an approach might in some cases lead to a situation where a large part of the male population of the former Yugoslavia was excluded from the reach of Article 5 even if they were targeted along with all the other members of their ethnic group. And we submit that could not have been the Security Council's intention in Article 5. And overwhelmingly, Your Honours, the concluded cases before this Tribunal have rejected such an approach. I'll touch on them only very briefly because they are referred to in our appeal brief and reply brief, but the Kordic Appeals Chamber in three separate instances included hors de combat victims amongst crimes against humanity convictions; the Naletilic Trial Chamber included forcing prisoners of war to perform work in dangerous conditions as part of the Article 5 convictions in that case; the Krstic and Blagojevic, the Srebrenica cases, provide further examples, where crimes against humanity convictions were entered in part in respect of crimes committed against the Bosnian Muslim 28th Division, which of course formed part of the column of men that was escaping Srebrenica and was ultimately captured and executed. And I can also add to this list the Fofana appeal judgement rendered by the Special Court of Sierra Leone, where crimes against humanity convictions were entered on appeal in that case and included crimes against captured enemy combatants, and I can refer Your Honours, for example, to paragraph 266, 321, and footnote 658 of that judgement and cross-referenced with the trial judgement. So, Your Honours, I submit that the result is clear. The question is: What is the reasoning that leads to this conclusion? And this brings me to the first part of my presentation today, which is our chapeau argument. We submit that individual victims of crimes against humanity need not be civilians as long as they are illegally targeted as part of a widespread or systematic attack that is directed against civilians. In essence, it's the widespread or systematic attack and not the individual acts of the accused that must target civilians. We accept, of course, that it's also necessary to determine that non-civilians have been harmed in a manner that is not lawful under international humanitarian law. We certainly do not advocate, for example, that lawful combat deaths under IHL could somehow be made unlawful under crimes against humanity. In your question in the Scheduling Order for today's hearing, you've asked the parties to address the Prosecution's chapeau argument specifically with reference to the wording of the chapeau in Article 5 and also with respect to the relevant jurisprudence. I'll start with the wording of the chapeau. And, Your Honours, I'll ask our case manager to bring this up on the screen for you because it's -- I think it's useful to see the wording of the Statute as we're going through this. And just as a general comment, Your Honours, I will be using quite a few slides during my presentation today, so you may wish to leave your monitors on, as that will help me go through it in a quicker manner. So, Your Honours, the wording of Article 5, the chapeau, is: "The International Tribunal shall have power to prosecute persons responsible for the following crimes when committed in armed conflict, whether international or internal in character, and directed against any civilian population ..." Do these words "and directed against any civilian population" mean that the underlying acts of the accused, the murder, torture, rape, and so on must be directed at civilian victims? We submit that the drafters of the Statute did not intend for Article 5 to be interpreted in that way, and I refer Your Honours to the report of the Secretary-General on the Statute of the Tribunal, and paragraph number 48, which will also appear on your screen, where the Secretary-General was commenting on Article 5, and he said in relevant part that: "Crimes against humanity refer to inhumane acts of a very serious nature, such as wilful killing, torture, or rape, committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against any civilian population ..." So the wording that the Secretary-General used here clarifies that the wording of the Statute was intended to convey that the attack rather than the individual acts of the accused must be directed against civilians. And we submit that this interpretation is confirmed in the wording of Article 3 of the ICTR Statute, which followed subsequently, and Article 3 states that: "The International Tribunal for Rwanda shall have power to prosecute persons responsible for the following crimes when committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against the civilian population ..." So this wording expressly reflects the interpretation of Article 5 that the Secretary-General gave in his report on this Tribunal's Statute. And we submit that this conclusion is also evident in the Secretary-General's report on the ICTR Statute because the Secretary-General commented on some of the differences in the wording between Article 5 of our Statute and Article 3 of the ICTR Statute, but he made no reference to this issue, and we submit that's because the wording in Article 3 was considered to be synonymous with the words "directed against any civilian population" in our Statute. The Appeals Chamber has confirmed that the phrase "directed against any civilian population" requires that the crimes be committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack against civilians. For example, the Tadic appeal judgement at paragraph 248 stated in relevant part that: " ... it may be inferred from the words 'directed against any civilian population' in Article 5 of the Statute that the acts of the accused must comprise part of a pattern of widespread or systematic crimes directed against a civilian population ..." And similarly in the Kunarac appeal judgement at paragraph 85, the Appeals Chamber affirmed that the chapeau requirement for Article 5 requires that the attack be directed against the civilian population. It did not specify that the individual acts of the accused must target civilians. Certainly, the Kunarac Appeals Chamber emphasized that in deciding whether an attack is directed primarily against civilians, it will of course be relevant to look at the status of the victims and their number, but there is nothing in the Kunarac appeal judgement that compels the conclusion that acts targeting non-civilians must be necessarily excluded. Can Article 5 be interpreted to mean that both the attack and the acts of the accused must be directed against civilians? And again, I'll ask Ms. Galicia to put up the wording of the Statute. We submit that the answer to that question must be no in light of the Appeals Chamber's case law. Your Honours, if the term "directed against any civilian population" was intended to qualify the acts of the accused, then it would be necessary to show not only that the acts of the accused were directed against civilians but also that they were directed against a 'population' in the sense of being part of a widespread or systematic -- in the sense of being a widespread or systematic course of events. For example, the Tadic trial judgement at paragraph 644 states that "the population element was included in Article 5 to imply crimes of a collective nature and so exclude isolated or single acts." But importantly, the Appeals Chamber has rejected the proposition that the acts of the accused must be widespread or systematic and has confirmed that a single act by an accused person can qualify as a crime against humanity if it is committed in the context of the broader attack. That's the Kunarac appeal judgement at paragraph 96 and the Blaskic appeal judgement at paragraph 101. So the point is really this, Your Honours: If the acts of the accused can be directed against a single victim, as long as they form part of the broader attack, then it logically follows that the acts of the accused need not necessarily target civilians as long as they form part of an attack directed against civilians. More generally, the Appeals Chamber's case law before both this Tribunal and the ICTR confirms that the victim acts of the accused need not share the required features of the broader attack. For example, the Appeals Chamber in the Kunarac case ruled that it does not matter whether the accused intended to target the civilian population as such or only his individual victim. In particular, in confirming the irrelevance of person motives in assessing the acts of the accused, the Kunarac Appeals Chamber stated at paragraph 103: "It is the attack, not the acts of the accused, which must be directed against the target population, and the accused need only know that his acts are part thereof." The case law of the ICTR Appeals Chamber provides a further example. In Article 3 of the ICTR Statute, there is an additional requirement that the widespread and systematic attack against the civilian population must also be committed on discriminatory grounds. In Akayesu, the Appeals Chamber ruled that the individual acts of the accused need not be committed on discriminatory grounds as long as they form part of a broader attack that is discriminatory. That's at paragraph 467 of the Akayesu appeal judgement. So as the Kayishema Trial Chamber put it at paragraph 135: "The crimes themselves need not contain the three elements of the broader attack under the ICTR Statute (that is, they need not be widespread or systematic, they need not be directed against civilians, and they need not be committed on discriminatory grounds, as long as they form part of an attack that meets all those requirements." Your Honours, we submit that the Appeals Chamber's application of Article 5 to the facts that have arisen in cases before it confirms that individual victims need not be civilians. In particular, in affirming Kordic's conviction for crimes against humanity in Santici, the Kordic Appeals Chamber stated at paragraph 480 that it included the killing of three identified victims, and it specifically stated that whether or not these individual victims were civilians was "beside the point." This must mean that individual victims of crimes against humanity needn't be civilians. The conclusion on the Santici analysis is confirmed in the Kordic Appeals Chamber's approach to crimes in Rotilj. The Appeals Chamber concluded that both to members and civilians were detained in Rotilj but that the majority were civilians and that there was an unlawful attack directed against civilians in that village, paragraphs 538 to 539 of the judgement. In convicting Kordic for murder as a crime against humanity, the Appeals Chamber noted that seven individuals had been killed in the village, but the Appeals Chamber importantly did not discuss their individual status as civilians. As the Appeals Chamber found at paragraph 543: "Taking into account that the killings occurred in the context of an unlawful attack on civilians, the Appeals Chamber considers that a reasonable trier of fact could have found that the elements of murder" as a crime against humanity "were established." The Martic Trial Chamber's conclusion, erroneous conclusion we would submit, that individual victims must be civilians was based on a misreading of the Blaskic appeal judgement. At paragraph 107 of that judgement, the Blaskic Appeals Chamber had stated in relevant part: "The Appeals Chamber considers that both the status of the victim as a civilian and the scale on which it is committed or the level of organization ... characterize a crime against humanity." Your Honours, this passage must be read in context. Here, the Appeals Chamber was discussing the chapeau requirement of Article 5 that the attack must be directed against civilians. The Appeals Chamber here, we submit, was simply saying that both the widespread or systematic character of the attack and the fact that the attack must be directed against a civilian population characterize the chapeau element. Your Honours, I also refer you to the Tadic appeal judgement at paragraph 286, and in this passage the Appeals Chamber was commenting on the relationship between Article 3 of the Statute and Article 5 of the Statute, and it said in relevant part that: " ... those who drafted the Statute deliberately included both classes of crimes," that is, war crimes and crimes against humanity, "thereby illustrating their intention that those war crimes which, in addition to targeting civilians as victims, present special features such as the fact of being part of a widespread or systematic practice, must be classified as crimes against humanity and deserve to be punished accordingly." To the extent that this could be read as suggesting individual victims must be civilians, we submit that it is inconsistent with later Appeals Chamber case law and that it should not be followed. I must also acknowledge Trial Chamber authorities before both this Tribunal and the ICTR that either expressly state or implicitly assume individual victims must be civilians. We have already cited a number of these in our reply brief in footnote 2, and to these I should add the following ICTR authorities: The Rutuganda trial judgement at paragraph 79 and the Akayesu trial judgement at paragraph 578, 582, and 589. We submit that these Trial Chamber authorities are inconsistent with the Appeals Chamber case law that I've described and which support the Prosecution's chapeau argument. A final question might arise for Your Honours concerning the chapeau argument. If crimes against civilians and non-civilians alike can qualify as crimes against humanity, what was the purpose of including the civilian requirement in Article 5 at all? Why insist on an attack against a civilian population if the individual victims can either be civilian or non-civilian? We submit that the requirement of an attack directed against a civilian population serves to rule out legitimate combat action. Although under customary international law crimes against humanity can of course occur in peacetime or in war, the fact remains that in Article 5 of our Statute we are applying it in or to the context of an armed conflict. To respect IHL's lex specialis status, we must ensure that lawful combat under IHL is not caught within the reach of Article 5; and that, we submit, is the purpose of including the civilian population requirement. Your Honours, this brings me to my second argument, the civilian definition argument. If, as we advocate under the chapeau argument, the civilian population requirement serves to rule out legitimate combat action, then it logically follows that the term "civilian" should be interpreted to mean people who are not lawful targets of attack under IHL, people whom it is not lawful to direct combat action against. As I said at the beginning of my submissions, the chapeau argument and the civilian definition argument are really mutually reinforcing arguments. And we submit that in this context the relevant IHL principle to take into Article 5 is that anyone who is not directly participating in the hostilities is protected from attack, and this is reflected in Common Article 3 to the Geneva Conventions and, of course, the principle of distinction, which underpins so much of international humanitarian law. These people covered by Common Article 3 are properly regarded as civilians in the specific sense in which that term is used in Article 5. Let me make it clear at the outset that when I say individuals not participating in the hostilities, I don't mean members of the armed forces who simply happen not to be engaged in combat or happen not to be armed at a particular point in time. We fully accept that as the Blaskic Appeals Chamber rightly found at paragraph 114, members of the armed forces remain lawful targets even when they are not engaged in combat or happen not to be armed. We mean non-combatants in the sense of Common Article 3, people who are protected from attack, including persons hors de combat because they've been rendered incapable of combat. By contrast, the Trial Chamber in this case defined civilians purely by reference to non-membership of the armed forces. And for reasons that I'll explain, we submit that was the wrong bench-mark to use in the context of Article 5, that it conflicts with the principle of distinction, and that it's contrary to the object and purpose of Article 5 as I've outlined in my submissions. We fully accept that IHL is an important bench-mark and an important reference point for defining the term "civilian" in Article 5. But we submit - and this is really the key point that I want to convey to Your Honours today - that the issue is more nuanced than simply identifying a corresponding label in IHL and transposing that into the distinctive Article 5 context. Instead, it's important to examine and to fully understand the concepts underpinning the labels in IHL and the purpose that they play in that particular regime and then to assess how appropriate it is to transfer them into the context of Article 5. It's a complex point, Your Honours, and I'm going to try and attempt to illustrate it with the aid of some diagrams because I think this is a case where pictures really do assist more than words. So what I have is a series of four charts that I'm going to put up on the monitors for Your Honours, and the first one is on your screens now, and I've called this: Article 5: Who Is a Civilian? And you can see there, Your Honours, that there are four boxes, four blue boxes, each numbered. And these boxes represent the various categories of people that we are concerned with in answering the question before you. So in box number 1, we have non-members of the armed forces not directly participating in hostilities; in the second box, we have non-members of the armed forces who are directly participating in the hostilities; in box 3, we have members of the armed forces not directly participating in the hostilities, and here we include persons hors de combat for the reasons I've explained; and in box 4, finally, we have members of the armed forces directly participating in the hostilities. So how should we classify each of these groups for Article 5 purposes? Well, box number 1 as demonstrated on the chart is not difficult. That's the easy part of this question. As the down arrow on the chart from box number 1 shows, these people are always non-combatants in IHL, and they are clearly civilians for Article 5 purposes. On the other side of the diagram in box number 4, members of the armed forces directly participating in the hostilities. To the extent that these people are enemy combatants who've been lawfully targeted in accordance with IHL, they are not civilians for Article 5 purposes. So for our purposes today, we can also exclude these from consideration. But as the chart shows with box number 2 and box 3, there is a question as to how to properly classify these other two groups of people. Let's consider what the Trial Chamber did in the present case, and this brings me to the second chart, which I've called: IHL's Technical Definition of Non-Combatant and Civilian. Again, we have the same four boxes from the previous chart representing our categories of people, and we can see that the Trial Chamber's approach was to classify as civilians the people in box number 1 and box 2. These are non-combatants or civilians in the technical meaning of Article 50 of Protocol I. It's a definition that reflects the fact that they are non-members of the armed forces who are not entitled to participate in the hostilities. So let me just go over some of the salient points that emerge from this chart. Why have I called it a technical definition? Well, it's technical because it reflects the particular characteristics of international armed conflicts, where combatant status, that term combatant, carries with it certain so-called privileges such as the right to use violent force without being subjected to punishment. States have clearly stipulated that only members of the armed forces are entitled to benefit from this privilege. And we see this reflected, for example, in Article 43(2) of Protocol I, which states that members of the armed forces of a party to the conflict ... are combatants, that is to say, they have the right to participate directly in hostilities." So it's a definition tied up with entitlement to participate, regardless of whether these people actually do participate or not. We fully accept that persons hors de combat remain as members of the armed forces combatants in this technical sense of Article 50. By contrast, non-members of the armed forces do not have these privileges, and they can be punished if they participate in the hostilities. So I submit, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber overlooked the purpose underlying the Article 50 civilian definition. It is not a definition that is synonymous with protected status under IHL. In particular, if non-members of the armed forces, the people in box number 2, do participate in the hostilities, under Article 50 they retain their civilian status but they lose their protection from attack as set out, for example, in Article 51(3) of Additional Protocol I. So as this chart shows, in adopting the Article 50 approach the Trial Chamber has included in the definition of "civilian" the people in box number 2 who are actually lawful targets of attack under IHL. The Trial Chamber also overlooked the fact - and this is the second problem that we see with the Trial Chamber's approach - that there is another concept of non-combatant in IHL regulating both international and internal armed conflicts, and we can see this reflected in the next slide which I've called: IHL's Generic Definition of Non-Combatant/Civilian. Again, we have the same four boxes representing the categories of people at issue, but here what we see is that box number 1 and box 3 make up non-combatants in the generic sense in which that term is used. And I use the word "generic" because it's a term that has been used in this context in the ICRC customary law study, and I'll explain a little bit more about that in a moment. This concept of non-combatant is reflected in Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, and it conveys the important fact for Article 5 purposes that these are people who are protected from attack under IHL. Persons hors de combat in box number 3 are regarded as non-combatants in this generic sense. They are protected from attack as set out, for example, in Article 41 of Protocol I. In this context, even in IHL, persons hors de combat are assimilated with civilians who do not participate in the hostilities and are protected from attack. So, for example, the ICRC commentary to Article 41 of Protocol I at paragraph 1605 states that: "It is a fundamental principle of the law of war that those who do not participate in the hostilities shall not be attacked. In this respect, harmless civilians and soldiers hors de combat are a priori on the same footing." Other sources also underscore that persons hors de combat are non-combatants in this generic sense of the term. For example, as we've referred to in our appeal brief at paragraph 31, persons hors de combat are referred to as non-combatants in both the drafting history and the commentary to Article 41 of Protocol I. Military manuals also reflect this conclusion. For example, the US Law on Naval Operations, 1995, at section 11.1 states that: "Non-combatants are non-members of the armed forces who do not participate in the hostilities," so our box number 1, people, "and members of the armed forces who enjoy special protected status, including persons who have been rendered incapable of combat by wounds, sickness, shipwreck, or capture." In other words, persons hors de combat are people in box number 3. And as I've said, the best articulation of this generic concept of non-combatant is Common Article 3 which is an intransgressible benchmark applicable in all conflicts. And that, we say, Your Honours, is the correct concept to take from IHL in defining who is a civilian for Article 5 purposes. Why do we say this? It's because this generic concept of non-combatant is consistent with the principle of distinction, which is as I've mentioned such a key foundation of IHL. And I'll ask the case manager to put up the next slide. This is the final in the series of slides: Article 5, Definition of Non-Combatant/Civilian. And here what I've tried to do is to reflect all the relevant concepts from the previous slides so that you can see it in one place. You can see the bold lines going down to the box on the right-hand side shows what we submit is the correct approach, the generic meaning of non-combatants from Common Article 3. And the dotted lines going down to the box on the left-hand side is the Martic Trial Chamber approach using the technical meaning from Article 50. I've said that the approach we advocate for is consistent with the principle of distinction, and the ICRC customary law study really underscores this conclusion. In Rule number 1 which is set out in volume 1, page 3 of the study, the ICRC define the principle of distinction as requiring parties to the conflict to "at all times distinguish between civilians and combatants. Attacks must not be directed at civilians." But in commenting on this rule, the authors of the study emphasize that the term "combatant" in this rule must be understood in its "generic" sense, meaning people who do not have protection from attack. And the authors go on to say, and the quote will come up on your screens: "This rule has to be read in conjunction with the prohibition to attack persons recognised to be hors de combat and with the rule that civilians are protected against attack unless and for such time as they take a direct part in hostilities." So again, if we return back to the last slide, the Martic Trial Chamber - and subsequently this approach was also adopted by the Mrksic Trial Chamber - erred in finding that their definitions of civilian were necessary to safe-guard the principle of distinction. We submit that it's the conception of non-combatant set out in Common Article 3, not Article 50 of Protocol I, that is consistent with the principle of distinction. Your Honours, we do not pretend that you will find the label civilian used anywhere in IHL to describe persons hors de combat, and there is a very good reason for that, because they are their own category of analysis in the rather complex and multi-layered framework of protection provided by IHL. But when it comes to the distinctive framework of Article 5 with just this simple distinction being made between civilians and non-civilians and bearing in mind the objective of that term being to exclude lawful combat, we submit that it is the approach in Common Article 3 that is the correct concept to take from IHL into Article 5. As we've explained in our appeal brief at paragraphs 19 to 20 and reply brief at 12 to 16, the Kordic Appeals Chamber has confirmed that persons hors de combat are civilians in the sense of Article 5. This is consistent with voluminous case law of the Trial Chambers at both this Tribunal and also the ICTR, which have adopted the Common Article 3 approach to this question. We have cited ten such authorities in our appeal brief at footnotes 31 and 32, and to this list I add the Krnojelac trial judgement at paragraph 56, the Krajisnik trial judgement at paragraph 706, and the Haradinaj trial judgement at paragraph 107. And the case law of the ICTR also underscores this position. It's too voluminous to go through each case now, but I can safely say that almost uniformly the ICTR Chambers have adopted the Common Article 3 approach to the definition of civilians. The Martic Trial Chamber erroneously relied on the Galic and the Blaskic appeal judgements to conclude that the term civilian in Article 5 should be defined exclusively in accordance with Protocol I. In our appeal brief, we've explained why in our view neither of those judgements compel that result, and I won't repeat the argument today, but I would just note that our reading of the Appeals Chamber's case law, in particular the Blaskic appeal judgement, is supported by the Krajisnik Trial Chamber at paragraph 706 and the Haradinaj Trial Chamber at paragraph 107. In conclusion, Your Honours, we ask you to find that persons hors de combat can be included in the Article 5 victim group because individual victims need not be civilians, our chapeau argument; and because persons hors de combat are properly regarded as civilians in the specific context of Article 5. We also submit that in resolving this case it's not necessary for Your Honours to attempt a monolithic definition of the term "civilian" for Article 5 purposes, and there is of course always an inherent danger in trying to do that because new issues will arise in other cases that need to be taken into account that perhaps have not been foreseen at this stage. And, for example, I could mention that there may be an issue about the particular status of members of the armed forces who are participating in hostilities but who have been targeted by their own side to the conflict and so perhaps in that context couldn't be regarded as enemy combatants. But it's sufficient for the purposes of this case to recognise that those people who do not participate in the hostilities as set out in Common Article 3, including persons hors de combat, are certainly included. Your Honours, I'm available for any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Ms. Jarvis, subject to what your colleague Mr. Milovancevic will say, I find your arguments interesting; but tell me this: You have said, I gather, that crimes against humanity do not have the restricted meaning which they had in the post-war period that they have absorbed, so to speak, the developments in human rights law. Possibly, I shall find the answer to my question from a perusal of your arguments and from your written briefs. But tell me, have you given any authorities in support of that proposition?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, we have addressed this matter in our reply brief, and there are really a couple of points to note. And one of them, I guess, is -- it's not an authority, but it's a contextual comment, which I'll begin with, and then I'll move into the authorities that might assist Your Honour with this point. We understand that when the crimes against humanity concept was inserted into the Nuremberg charter, that part of the rationale was because crimes against the civilian population, the parties to the conflicts' own civilian population weren't covered by the reach of war crimes provisions. So this was a vehicle for addressing that shortcoming. But what I said at the beginning of my submissions was that by 1991 we'd moved on quite a long way from that, both because of the influence of human rights developments which had absorbed, as Your Honour aptly put it, the crimes against humanity doctrine, but also because war crimes provisions themselves had expanded so that now we do have war crimes protections covering civilians even when targeted by a party or their own state, if you like. We've developed in that sense, so the framework of viewing these two doctrines as supplementary, if you like, rather than overlapping has really changed, fundamentally changed, by 1991. And that's reflected, we submit, in the fact that the doctrine of crimes against humanity as we find it being developed by the early 1990s had not incorporated any longer the civilian population requirement. In tandem with the armed conflict nexus requirement, the civilian population requirement, we submit, had really dropped out of customary international law. Let me explain why I say that. First of all, we have to understand that the civilian population limitation, even in the immediate post-World War II era, was a limited one for the Nuremberg charter in Control Council Law number 10. It only related to non-persecution-type crimes against humanity. So for persecution as a crime against humanity, it was never limited by a civilian population requirement. We also know that the Tokyo Charter, although when first drafted, it included the civilian population limitation in the same way as the Nuremberg Charter. Before that Tribunal actually commenced operating, the Statute or the Charter was amended to eliminate this requirement and, we've referred to the various authorities in our reply brief. We also know that subsequent articulations of the doctrine of crimes against humanity, for example, in the apartheid convention, the genocide convention, did not include any civilian population limitation. And we submit that in large part the state practice that we've relied on in our reply brief in support of this position that the customary law requirements had changed is in large part the very same state practice that the Appeals Chamber has relied on to find that the armed conflict nexus had been eliminated as part of customary international law. And we've also referred to the IOC's work on crimes against humanity in 1991 and 1996, which formulated the doctrine without reference to a civilian population limitation. It was by that time a doctrine that was about condemning widespread or systematic practices of human rights abuses. So for that reason we say there is no problem in terms of customary international law or the principle of legality in the approach that we are suggesting. What Your Honours are confronted with is a situation where you have to interpret Article 5 of the Statute in light of its object and purpose, and that we say is why you should take the concept from Common Article 3 into Article 5 because that's the most apt, relevant concept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other questions? Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I ask you this question as a follow-up. Now, we know that the Security Council cannot expand on the province covered by customary international law, but can it do the reverse? Can it cut down the jurisdiction vested in this Tribunal? Can it say that, all right, under those treaties to which you have referred the civilian population element has been effectively deleted, but see here, we will put it back just to cut down the jurisdiction which you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Security Council absolutely can make the provisions of our Statute more restrictive than customary international law, and we've seen that, for example, in Article 5 with the armed conflict requirement. So certainly that is true, and I would submit another example is, of course, the ICTR Statute, Article 3, which includes the requirement of the discriminatory intent for the -- for crimes against humanity, which our Tribunal has rejected as part of customary international law. So there's no question on that score, but that really leads us to the very premise of my submissions, and that is it's not a matter of the principle of legality. This is a requirement that has been put into the Statute by the Security Council. What was intended? Was it really intended to limit the application of the doctrine in a way that doesn't make sense in contemporary times that perhaps made sense at the time of the Nuremberg Charter but no longer? Or can it not be sensibly interpreted in a way that makes the crimes against humanity doctrine a living, breathing doctrine relevant to our times by saying what it means is, Let's exclude lawful combat because we know that we cannot, having regard to IHL's lex specialis status, make something unlawful under Article 5 that is lawful under IHL. And that's the very essence of our argument, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I had no microphone. I give the floor back to the Prosecution. You have a few minutes to conclude your arguments.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think Ms. Nabti is prepared to make her submissions briefly, and we appreciate the opportunity to just wrap up on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NABTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I will very briefly address Your Honours on the relief requested by the Prosecution on its ground of appeal. The Prosecution asks the Appeals Chamber to apply the correct legal standard and to find that the hors de combat victims identified in our appeal were also victims of the Article 5 crimes at issue, and it can do so based on the Trial Chamber's findings on the elements of those crimes. The Prosecution further requests the Appeals Chamber to ensure that Martic's sentence reflects the totality of the criminal conduct for which he stands convicted on appeal. As set out in section 2A of the Prosecution's appeal brief, our appeal concerns hors de combat victims of two crime base groups: The murder victims of the 18 November 1991 attack on Skabrnja, and victims of detention-related crimes. The seven hors de combat murder victims identified in our appeal were targeted together with other villagers who were forced out of their homes and killed or who were otherwise executed by gun-shots to the head at close or point-blank range. Those findings are at paragraphs 251, 254, 256, and 259 of the trial judgement and accompanying footnotes. Similarly, the hors de combat detainees at the three detention facilities at issue in our appeal, the JNA 9th Corps barracks, the old hospital in Knin, and the Tetova Korenica SJB were kept in detention and were mistreated together with everyone else and were likewise discriminated against on the basis of their ethnicity. Those findings are at paragraphs 283, 288, 411, and 416 of the trial judgement. As my colleague Ms. Baig clarified yesterday, at trial the Prosecution did not seek convictions, and we therefore do not seek a remedy for the mistreatment of two hors de combat detainees while at the Benkovac SJB before they were later transferred to the old hospital in Knin. Based on the Trial Chamber's findings on the elements of the crimes, the Appeals Chamber should enter a conviction for these crimes against humanity with respect to the hors de combat victims, and these findings have already made with -- by the Trial Chamber. In finding that the general requirements for Article 5 had been met at paragraphs 438 -- I'm sorry, 348 to 353 of the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber considered the crimes committed against hors de combat victims to form part of the wide and systematic attack directed against the civilian population. The Trial Chamber also made sufficient findings that the constituent elements of the underlying offences of persecution, murder, torture, and inhumane acts were met with respect to the hors de combat victims. These findings are at paragraphs 387 and 390 for murder; 408, 413, and 418 for torture and inhumane acts; and 411 and 416 for persecution. The Prosecution does not seek cumulative convictions for the inter-Article 5 crimes of torture and inhumane acts following the Trial Chamber's findings regarding cumulative convictions at paragraphs 474 to 477. Finally, with respect to the sentence we ask the Appeals Chamber simply to consider this enlarged victim group of the relevant crimes against humanity convictions. Whether or not the Prosecution appeal -- Prosecution's appeal results in an actual increase of the sentence, consideration of the gravity of Martic's convictions on appeal is appropriate in order to ensure that his sentence accurately and comprehensively reflects his criminal culpability, including the full scale of the crimes against humanity of which he is ultimately found guilty. Unless there are any questions, that concludes my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Well, now, thank you for those submissions. I will now turn to the Defence for their submissions. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my colleague, Mr. Perovic, will present the arguments of the Defence of this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. It is my intention to spend the following 45 minutes trying to convince you that the arguments presented by the Prosecution are unfounded, and in doing so I will strictly abide by the instructions of the Appeals Chamber. The essence of the arguments of the Prosecution can be seen in the first paragraph of their appeal brief where they claim that the Trial Chamber made an error in law when it concluded that the persons hors de combat cannot be considered victims of crimes against humanity under Article 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal. It is the claim of the Prosecution that persons hors de combat, even though they are members of armed forces of a warring side, cannot be considered the target of the attack, lawful target of the attack, and thus should be considered as civilians. The Prosecution claims that even though persons hors de combat cannot be considered civilians, even if that is found, they still should be considered victims of crimes against humanity. I will now respond to the arguments presented by the Prosecution, and to the extent possible I will try to avoid repeating the arguments that can be found in our brief. In our response brief, we invoked such cases as Mrksic, Radic, Sljivancanin trial judgement and Blaskic appeals judgement. The jurisprudence of the ICTY is not consistent when it comes to certain fundamental issues of humanitarian law and international criminal law, such as the scope of crimes against humanity; or to be more precise, whether members of armed forces who are hors de combat can be considered victims of crimes against humanity. A proper understanding of the term "civilian" and "civilian population" is something that the international humanitarian law is based upon as well as international criminal law. It is quite surprising for me that these fundamental issues seem to be contentious in the case law of the Tribunal. It is beyond dispute that persons who are hors de combat need to be treated humanely under all circumstances and that inhumane acts against them are crime under international law. This is not contentious. It is also beyond dispute that persons hors de combat are protected persons, since they are not able or they have no right to actively participate in hostilities. As a result of that, these persons cannot be legal or lawful targets of an attack. In other words, it is the general rule of law that in every armed conflict the right of warring sides to choose means and manners of engaging in hostilities is not unrestricted and that the protection of hors de combat persons is one of the limitations to limit means and manner of conducting hostilities which is regulated by international customary law and international treaty law, including Common Article 3 of Geneva Conventions and Article 41 of the Additional Protocol I. However, case law of the Tribunal introduces certain confusion when it comes to the legal concept and status of hors de combat persons. And as a preliminary issue which is very important in establishing whether these persons can be victims of crimes against humanity, we need to establish who can acquire the status of a person hors de combat. I think that it is beyond dispute that only members of armed forces can acquire the status of HDC. I reiterate that members of armed forces do not cease being members of armed forces if they are wounded or unable for any other reason to participate in the combat, and they can also be held accountable for war crimes or crimes against humanity. The case law of this Tribunal is not clear on the issue whether persons hors de combat can be considered civilians when it comes to the application of Article 5 of the Statute. It is the position of the OTP that hors de combat persons can be considered victims of crimes against humanity. The OTP bases this argument on partially case law of the Tribunal and teleological interpretation of Article 5 of the Statute. On the other hand, Defence in certain cases ignored this issue because - and this comes as a great surprise to me - we can see it in Jelesic, Limaj, and Tadic cases, the position of the Trial Chamber in those cases was not appealed. The case law of both Trial Chambers and Appeals Chambers is contradictory when it comes to the legal concept of the status of hors de combat persons under Article 5 of the Statute. In the Jelesic case, it was stated that based on the spirit and text of the Article 5, this concept needs to be broadly interpreted. In the text, it says that these acts were against any members of civilian population, the emphasis being the collective nature of this crime rather than the nature of the victims. The Security Council believed that Article 5 needs to cover all persons who were under arms but were not, strictly speaking, necessarily involved in armed activities. As a result, they concluded that in addition to civilians in the narrow sense, Article 5 also encompasses everybody who was hors de combat when the crime was committed, or as was stated in the trial judgement in the Krnojelac case - I'm quoting - "the definition of civilians is expansive, and it includes individuals who during one point of time were involved in resistance as well as persons hors de combat who had that status after the crime was committed." In the Mrksic judgement, as was pointed out, that in the case law of the Tribunal so far the term "civilian" was defined only in the context of general conditions for applying Article 5 of the Statute, the conditions that existed when the attack aimed against civilians were carried out. Based on the various judgements that I just quoted, one can see that the term "civilian" was inappropriately broadly interpreted. The conclusion of the Trial Chamber in the Mrksic case cannot be used as an adequate explanation of the case law of the Tribunal prior to that when it comes to qualification of the hors de combat persons as civilians for the purposes of application of Article 5 of the Statute because as we will explain a little bit later and as was confirmed in the appeals judgement in the Blaskic case and the trial judgement in the Mrksic case, I'm quoting: "Members of armed forces and members of police and voluntary units which form part of such armed forces cannot be entitled to the status of civilians, just like members of organized resistance groups cannot be considered civilians." It is the position of the Defence that the Trial Chamber in the Mrksic case was quite right, namely, that when it comes to application of Article 5 victims need to be civilians. If the victims are not civilians, then they -- the more appropriate charge would be the war crimes charge. The Chamber believes that this is an adequate and special condition for the application of Article 5, which takes into account historical sources, the development of the crime against humanity, which is a crime in a different category from war crimes category. The issues raised by the Prosecution in their appeal show a number of inconsistencies when it comes to the number of trial judgements where it was said that for the purposes of the application of Article 5 of the Statute, persons hors de combat need to be considered civilians. Up until the appeals judgement in the Blaskic case, the Appeals Chamber did not have opportunity to rule on this issue; however, this issue seems to be problematic because in the Limaj case on the 30th of November the trial -- the 30th of November, 2005, which came after the appeals case -- appeals judgement in Blaskic case, the Trial Chamber was of the view that the definition of civilians was expansive and included persons who were hors de combat when the crime was committed. And to add a bit more of confusion, in the appeals judgement in the Galic case, it was stated that it would not be necessarily correct to say that persons hors de combat were civilians in the context of international humanitarian law. I seem to be having problems with interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: This has now been resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Now it's okay. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Contrary to the inconsistent jurisprudence before the Tribunal, Article 5 of the Tribunal is more than clear, and it reads as follows in the relevant part: "The International Tribunal shall have the power to prosecute persons responsible for the following crimes when they're committed in armed conflict, either international or internal in character, directed against the civilian population." It follows from this that the civilian status of a victim is a general requirement for the application of Article 5 of the Statute. The text of Article 5 is in line with international customary law. The certain acts that are in violation of international customary and treaty law protecting the civilian populations against the horrors of law are incriminated in Article 5. The violations of certain provisions of the Nuremberg -- enshrined in the Nuremberg Charter, the Statute of the present Tribunal, and of the ICC define crimes against humanity as inhumane acts or acts of persecution committed against the civilian population. To illustrate that in order to see how the protected subject is defined of crimes against humanity, we can quote from the UN commission, International Law Commission findings where it says that definitions from the Charters of the Nuremberg and Tokyo Tribunals and the Control Council Law 10 for Germany, the -- it has been concluded that crimes against humanity, such as murder, are crimes committed against the civilian population. Crimes committed against members of the armed forces were outside of the scope and probably outside of the scope of the crimes against humanity of the type of persecution. Or, as it was noted in the same report, I quote: "The words civilian population appear to include the notion that crimes against humanity are limited to inhumane acts against civilian population, not against members of the armed forces." In this specific case, this is what the Trial Chamber found in the Mrksic case. What is contentious here is the definition of the civilian, which must be applied, and since Article 5 of the Statute is quite clear and that only civilian population can be a victim of the crime -- of a crime against humanity, the question is whether crimes against humanity may be committed against a member of the armed forces, and this in my opinion is irrelevant for the purposes of interpretation of this Article. At any rate, international instruments, international laws, confirm the finding that only civilian population can be victim of crimes against humanity. Contrary to the conclusions of the United Nations War Crimes Commission, explicitly in Article 6 of the Nuremberg Charter, it is stipulated -- or rather, the Supreme Court in the British occupational zone took the position at least three times that military personnel can be considered as victims of crimes against humanity. So this is contrary to the findings of the UN War Crimes Commission and the explicit stipulation in Article 6(C) of the Nuremberg Charter. There is a decision of the French Cessation Court from 1985, but it can hardly be considered to support the position of the Prosecution that members of the armed forces can be victims of crimes against humanity. It says in this decision that crimes -- victims of crimes against humanity may be opponents of a certain policy regardless of the way they mount their resistance, but this judgement does not elaborate whether members of armed forces can be victims of crimes against humanity. Jurisprudence of other courteous seems to be unanimous regarding a narrow, restricted interpretation of the term "civilian" and "civilian population"; and as Antonio Cassese noted, the term -- notion of crimes against humanity excludes persons that belong or belonged to the armed forces. Let me just give you some more case law of national courts. The courts set up in occupational zones in Germany were not international, and their jurisprudence has to be treated as domestic case law. It cannot be used as an authority because according to the status of the -- Statute of the Tribunal the civilian status of the victim is a prerequisite for the application of Article 5. On the other hand, domestic and international law may diverge here. The states are under an obligation to prosecute certain crimes in their domestic legislation. They are unanimous about the goals that must be achieved but not unanimous about the instruments, how this must be achieved. So despite this divergence there can be harmony. States are under an obligation to incriminate certain crimes, but the labels they affix may be different. But the factual situation and legal qualifications can differ from those that exist in international law. International courts must comply with their founding acts and are not bound by domestic law. The interpretation of Article 5 of the Statute must be done in accordance with the legal practice, lege artis, in other words. Customary law codified in Article 31 of the Vienna Convention on Treaty Law stipulates that treaties must be interpreted bona fide in accordance with the usual interpretation of the terms used in treaties and their context and in light of their object and purpose. And special meaning may be given to some terms only if it is found that this was the intention of the parties. In addition to this rule, the rule of narrow interpretation must be given when international criminal law provisions are interpreted when this is recognised by the international community. And also the civilizational --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the counsel please read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to read as slowly as I can. Quote from Article 22 of the International Criminal Court reads: "When there is any ambiguity, the definition will be interpreted in favour of the person under investigation on trial or person who has already been convicted. In dubio pro reo is one of the key notions of every criminal law including international criminal law. The Statute of the Tribunal is not a treaty. It is a unilateral act of the UN Security Council, and that is why this was not an intention of the states that must be taken into account but the intention of the Security Council when it is being interpreted. But since the Security Council is not an organ of the United Nations that has legislative powers, in extreme cases it can only reproduce in its instruments those rules and principles of international law that are already in force. In other words, no progressive development or divergence from the generally accepted treaty law rules is permissible here. In this specific case, there is no ambiguity. Everything is clear. What we're dealing with is an attempt to expand the term "civilians" in an artificial manner. The terms "civilian" and "civilian population" defined in Article 50 of Additional Protocol I, to reflect the generally accepted and customary rules of international law in the Blaskic appeals judgement led to a proper conclusion that when the scope of the term "civilian population" is to be determined, the Appeals Chamber would like to remind that it is under obligation to determine the current status of customary law that was in force when crimes were committed. And in this regard, it notes that in the report of the Secretary-General it is noted that the Geneva Conventions, and I quote: "Make the rules of international humanitarian law and are the very core of international customary law that applies to armed conflict." Article 50 of Additional Protocol I contains the definition of civilians and civilian population, and provisions in that article can be considered an expression or codification of customary law. That is why they are relevant when we are discussing Article 5 in relation to crimes against humanity. That is why it can be concluded as follows: It was not the intention of the drafters of the Statute of the Tribunal to expand the notion of crime -- of civilians and civilian population for the purposes of crimes against humanity to go beyond what was determined in the international humanitarian and customary law, nor were the drafters of the Statute authorised to expand this notion of civilian. And it follows beyond reasonable doubt that members of the armed forces cannot be entitled to the status of a civilian in any sense or form. The teleological interpretation of Article 5 of the Statute, the teleological interpretation does not support the conclusion that persons hors de combat are civilians in the sense of crimes against humanity because members of armed forces even when they are wounded, imprisoned, captured, or rendered hors de combat for any other reason remained members of the armed forces. The letter and spirit of Article 5 of the Statute are quite clear. Only civilians can be victims of crimes against humanity, and it is not contentious that the Tribunal is bound by treaty and customary law that were in force at the time when the alleged crimes were committed. The object of legal protection of crimes against humanity are civilians or civilian population. This was explicitly envisaged not only in the Statute of the Tribunal but also in Article 6(C) of Nuremberg Charter as well as Article 7 of the Statute of ICC. The argument stating that crimes against humanity are inhumane acts which by their scope and gravity go beyond limits that international community may tolerate and for which punishment needs to be sought, and similar arguments cannot be used to support the claim that inhumane acts against hors de combat persons need to be qualified as crimes against humanity. Such acts may be qualified as war crimes or grave violations of the Geneva Conventions, and the incrimination of both war crimes, crimes against humanity, and grave breaches of Geneva Conventions were based or was based on similar moral and legal principles that have been in existence for a long time and which support the principles, norms, and rules which humanise or give human nature, give human element, to armed conflicts. Considerations which must be identical for all crimes that can be committed during armed conflicts cannot be used as arguments that certain crimes are crimes against humanity because crimes against humanity and war crimes are based on human considerations. However, there are differences among them or between them, and in order to establish whether a crime against humanity was committed one must determine inter alia whether the crime was committed against civilian population. It needs to be reiterated in the context of historical development of international criminal law and international humanitarian law, one needs to look in the basic differences when it comes to motive for protecting civilian population on the one hand and members of armed forces on the other hand. Civilian population needs to be protected because it is not entitled, authorised, to take direct part in hostilities. The motivation for protecting members of armed forces who are hors de combat, as Sir Hersch Lauterpacht stated, is based on the idea of chivalrous behaviour because it includes respect that combatants show towards their opponents as human beings. It is perhaps of importance for the case law of the Tribunal to resolve the issue of whether there could be differences in definition of civilians and civilian protection based on the nature of armed conflict. Historically speaking, the difference was made between internal and international conflicts, and up until recently internal conflicts fell under the internal jurisdiction of each state. Gradually, states agreed to apply certain rules of the international humanitarian law in non-international armed conflicts. Current state of law is such that many rules are equally applied, both in international and internal armed conflicts. There is, indeed, a problem there because numerous rules of international humanitarian law, even international criminal law, were created following the model of international armed conflict. The basis for regulating internal, non-international armed conflicts is Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions, which envisages minimal guarantees for protection of persons which do not actively participate in hostilities. However, bearing in mind the nature of internal, non-international conflicts, which can go from minor disruptions to real, full-blown civil wars, there could be a problem in identifying the rules of the international humanitarian law that need to be applied. This problem -- or rather, the problem of applicability of international humanitarian law in various situations is definitely resolved in Article 1 of Additional Protocol II. So the rules of international humanitarian law are applied in non-international armed conflicts, conflicts which are characterized by the fact that they occur between organized armed groups which are under responsible command. This is a common feature, both of international and non-international armed conflicts, and it is precisely this feature that is the prerequisite for application of the rules which regulate conduct of hostilities. Precisely due to this feature, a large number of identical rules is applied both in international and non-international armed conflicts. Bearing this in mind as well as that Protocol II does not contain the definition of the notion of civilian and civilian population, the prerequisites for application of this same definition in non-international and international armed conflicts have been met. Article 5 of this Statute provides that crimes against humanity can be committed in an armed conflict, be it an international or non-international one, and at the same time it doesn't make any difference between the variation of the elements of the crime against humanity based on the nature of the conflict. This clearly says that terms "civilian" and "civilian population" have identical meaning, regardless of the nature of the armed conflict, regardless of whether it's an internal or an international conflict. Part 4 of Additional Protocol II regulates the guarantee of the rights of civilian individuals and civilian population. These rules are of customary nature and represent codification of basic rules which apply to armed conflicts. These rules are identical to the rules which are applied in international armed conflicts, and all of them are based on an initial premise or on a general rule that civilian population and every individual civilian are entitled to general protection from the danger resulting from military operations. Violations of these rules are condemned by states regardless of the nature of the underlying conflict. In addition to this, there were no attempts when it comes to terms "civilian" and "civilian population" to define these terms in a different way depending on whether the conflict is international or non-international. The fact that Additional Protocol II does not contain the definition of the word "civilian" does not make a difference. Both in international and in internal conflicts, the same rule applies, namely, that warring sides need to make a distinction at all times between civilians and combatants, and it is only organized groups under responsible command that are entitled to participate in hostilities. It seems that contemporary international humanitarian law tends to ensure that all participants of armed conflict be treated humanely and that civilian population in non-international armed conflicts needs to be equally protected as in international armed conflicts. When analysing the development of international humanitarian law and international criminal law, it would be absurd to speak about a broader definition of civilian population in non-international but rather in international conflict. When it comes to persons hors de combat who cannot be considered civilians for the purposes of Article 5 of the Statute, I will say as follows: The status of persons hors de combat and the status of civilians is significantly different. Certain rules that apply to civilians cannot be applied to persons hors de combat, as the Trial Chamber established in the Mrksic case. They said that persons hors de combat cannot be victims of detention. In accordance with Article 5 of the Statute, deportation cannot be committed against prisoners of war, which is one of the categories of hors de combat persons. The position of the Prosecution when it comes to whether persons hors de combat can be victims of crimes against humanity is almost identical to the positions taken by the Prosecution in the Mrksic case, which were rejected by the Trial Chamber in the judgement in that case. The Prosecution errs in not making sufficient difference between the status of civilians and protected persons. For the purposes of application of Article 5 of the Statute, the Prosecution believes these terms to be synonymous. However, it is clear that a crime against humanity can be committed only against civilians but not against other categories of protected persons. It is a general rule that persons who do not actively participate in hostilities are considered protected persons. In addition to civilians, there are numerous other categories of other persons who are protected, including members of armed forces who are hors de combat. It is beyond any doubt that all persons who do not participate in hostilities are considered protected persons and that certain acts which are carried out against them are crimes under international law. However, not everybody who does not take part in hostilities is a civilian. It is true that Common Article 3 and Additional Protocol II are both focused on the difference between the persons who take part in hostilities and those who do not take active part in hostilities. However, Additional Protocol II has a separate part 4 regulating protection of civilian population, which is separate from protection accorded to other categories that are protected, such as hors de combat persons. Persons taking or not taking active part in hostilities are better terms to use now because to distinguish between combatants and civilians is not an exhaustive distinction. That is because not all members of the armed forces are combatants - for instance, medical personnel and religious personnel - because members of the armed forces cannot under any condition be accorded the status of civilians even when they're not combatants. On the other hand, in some conditions even civilians can be lawful targets of attacks. All those who do not take active part in hostilities are protected persons, but not all of these persons are civilians, nor can they be considered as victims of crimes against humanity. The fact that the Prosecution argument is unfounded can be seen from the fact that even members of the armed forces who are not entitled to take direct part in hostilities fall under the protection of Article 41 of Additional Protocol I, as noted in the commentary of the ICRC regarding this article. Medical and religious personnel and military personnel attached to the civilian protection do not have the right to take active part in hostilities so that when they fall under the power of the enemy side, or rather, when the enemy side is in a position to impose their will on them, it will do so without fighting and without changing their status to that of the hors de combat. So they enjoy protection under Article 41 regardless of protection they enjoy under other provisions of the Geneva Conventions and Additional Protocols. The same applies to unarmed soldiers, regardless of whether they might be caught by surprise while they're sleeping by the enemy or while they're on leave or in any other similar circumstances. It is quite obvious that the protection applies only when and only for as long as those persons abstained from acts of hostility and are not trying to flee. So it is quite clear that even those who are not combatants, those who do not have the right to directly take part in hostilities and, indeed, do not do so may be considered hors de combat, or at any rate they cannot be considered civilians in order to achieve any purpose, and they cannot, therefore, be considered as victims of crimes against humanity. I have one minute to wrap up, Your Honours. The argument that the term "civilian" under Article 5 of the Statute does not have the same meaning as the meaning of the term "civilian" in the Additional Protocol I cannot be accepted for the above-mentioned reasons. Furthermore, crimes against humanity in Article 5 of the Statute, that's -- these are general provisions whose meaning can be seen only in the context of international humanitarian law. In other words, the purpose of the incriminations of the crimes against humanity, war crimes, and grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions is to punish violations of customary and treaty law governing armed conflict and international humanitarian law. Under international law, the terms "civilian," "civilian population," "protected persons," and so on have their clear meaning, and there is no reason nor was this intention expressed by the states to ascribe or attribute any special meaning in order to punish any violations of international humanitarian law. And to conclude, it is beyond any doubt that members of the armed forces hors de combat are protected persons, but they're not civilians, and as such they cannot be considered as victims of crimes against humanity. And I'm -- this concludes my presentation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. Judge Schomburg, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, let me thank both parties for their attempt to give us some guidance in order to harmonize the jurisprudence of this International Tribunal and in doing so painting neither black or white, but really go in depth into the details of their arguments. But the question how best to interpret the chapeau elements of Article 5. My first question would be, in passing you mentioned the principle of in dubio pro reo. The scope of the application of this principle is disputed, no doubt; however, do you have any authority for the application of this principle, in dubio pro reo, when it comes to interpretation of statutory law opposed to apply this principle of in dubio pro reo solely to the fact-finding mission of a court? Sir, you mentioned several times civilians and civilian population, but isn't it true that it makes a difference whether it reads civilians or civilian population? Isn't it true that the direction of the attack is decisive, in particular under a teleological interpretation, taking into account object and purpose of Article 5; and to be very direct, isn't it true that a person hors de combat becomes, when he has gained this status, again, member of the civilian population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that in my reply to the Prosecution appeal I presented why it was impossible for persons who are members of the armed forces and who, for some reason, have been rendered hors de combat or are not participating in hostilities cannot be considered civilians. As far as the term "civilian" and "civilian population" is concerned, I believe that there is no difference. So we can consider those to be synonymous for all intents and purposes. I am unable to see any major difference between the two terms, "civilian" and "civilian population." As far as the principle in dubio pro reo is concerned, I consider this to be one of the key principles of criminal law in general, including international criminal law, and it should be applied whenever there is a possibility to do so. And this goes, also, for the application of Article 5 of the Statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Before giving the floor to Judge Shahabuddeen, I think we have to -- I'm advised that we have to break for five minutes only to change a tape. It's a technical matter. So I suspend for five minutes and we'll re-convene as soon as the tape is changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we resume the hearing. Judge Shahabuddeen, you wanted to put a question, I understand. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic, I want to thank you on my own behalf for a very able argument. I would want to ask you whether you think you have dealt adequately with the argument from your friend across the way. She distinguished between two concepts, the attack and the underlying crime. I gather she would not dispute your conception of the reference in Article 5 to civilian population, but I believe - I may be wrong - that she would confine the application of civilian population to the attack and would leave aside the question of the identification of the victim. Now, in that way I think she would tend to read the words "civilian population" as having, if I may say so, a jurisdictional import.
