She would see the reference, granted all that you say about its meaning, as confined to that question, that is the nature of the attack and not to the underlying crime. If I've got right the kernel of the presentation by the Prosecution, would you like to respond and to say whether you think you have dealt fully with her argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is the case. The key issue for me is what I said in -- by way of conclusion, whether members of the armed forces hors de combat can be considered as victims of crimes against humanity, victims of crimes against humanity. I believe, as I stated in my conclusion, that they cannot be in light of their capacity as members of the armed forces and their belonging to this category. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. I give now the floor to the Prosecution for their reply.

utterances.speaker: MS. JARVIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may perhaps just use a moment as I'm preparing to hand out for the Court and to my learned friend on the Defence copies of the slides, the four charts I used in my presentation today. Your Honours, I think I can try and be relatively brief by way of reply, but I do want to touch on a couple of the points my learned friend has raised as well as to add a couple of additional remarks that have been brought out by Your Honours' questions to the Defence. First of all, my learned friend referred to World War II case law that deals with the issue of whether individual -- whether crimes against humanity must exclude members of the armed forces, and I didn't touch upon that in my presentation today, but it is of course referred to in both our Prosecution appeal brief and our reply brief. And there are a series of World War II cases under Control Council Law number 10 which show that members of the armed forces can qualify as victims of crimes against humanity, particularly when targeted as part of a broader campaign of crimes. So I simply refer you to those parts of our brief and also perhaps to say as a supplement to my answer to Judge Shahabuddeen's question that these cases, of course, are also part of the package of material that evidences the evolution of crimes against humanity away from the civilian population requirement that we first saw in the Nuremberg Charter. The Defence also commented on the Barbi [phoen] case. I think it was the reference to the Court of Cessation of the French court. And again, we've addressed this in our brief, but we submit that it is clear from the outcome of that case that crimes against humanity were -- convictions were entered in respect of members of the armed forces, namely, members of the resistance, and that's particularly clear if you read the reasoning of the court and its rejection in particular of the lower court's reasoning, which had held that crimes against humanity are limited to crimes against non-combatants. So in rejecting that reasoning, we say that the court clearly affirmed the position that we take in the present case, namely, that victims can be both civilians and non-civilians. There is one point that I would really like to emphasize because it was drawn out both in the Defence submissions, but also in the question that Your Honour Judge Schomburg asked raising the issue of in dubio pro reo and its application to this question. And I think it's helpful to look once again at one of the slides, the final slide that I showed you, and you have your hard copies before you, and I think it will also come up on your screen. One of the key points I would like to emphasize is that the Prosecution's position on the definition of civilian is not that it should be defined in a more expansive way. I think as this final chart which is headed Article 5, Definition Of Non-Combatant and Civilian, really serves to demonstrate, our concern is that the Trial Chamber used the wrong bench-mark. It used box number 1 and 2. We say it should have used box number 1 and 3. In our brief, we've described this as a position that is -- that the Trial Chamber's definition was simultaneously too narrow and too broad at the same time: Too narrow because it excluded box 3; too broad because it included box 2. So our position really is not one of expansive interpretation; it really is about taking the correct concept from IHL having regard to the object and purpose of Article 5. Your Honours, the Defence also raised the issue of the rules regulating internal armed conflicts and pointed out that of course Article 5 doesn't draw a distinction between internal or international armed conflicts and that it applied -- the elements must be the same for both. Well, Your Honours, this is really the key to our argument because that's why we say Common Article 3, the base line provision applicable to all conflicts is the relevant guiding principle because indisputably, it applies regardless of the classification of the conflict. Another point I want to emphasize is something that arises out of the subsequent Mrksic Trial Chamber's approach on this issue, and my learned colleague referred to it. And the Mrksic Trial Chamber used the rationale that hors de combat persons cannot be victims of certain of the crimes laid out in Article 5. And I want to deal with this issue in two ways because we submit that this is not a relevant factor to consider in who is -- in defining who is a civilian. Let me first of all ask Your Honours to consider what the logical conclusion of the Mrksic Trial Chamber's own reasoning is on this point, and again, it's helpful to look at the fourth of my charts, which sets out the two approaches. The Mrksic Trial Chamber's approach, the Martic Trial Chamber's approach, and Article 50 include as we can see non-members of the armed forces who are directly participating in the hostilities. These people, as we know, are legitimate targets of attack. These people could not be victims of murder or other inhumane acts relating to bodily harm inflicted on them. So the Mrksic's Trial Chamber own reasoning breaks down at that point because in fact people that they have included in the civilian population definition cannot be victims of some of the underlying crimes against humanity such as murder and inhumane acts. I would also just express a note of caution about jumping too quickly to any conclusion that members of the armed forces cannot be victims of crimes like imprisonment or deportation. Certainly the circumstances under which they could be victims of those crimes might be different because of the corresponding IHL provisions, but we should not hastily jump to the conclusion that they could never be victims. For example, an imprisonment which starts off as lawful under IHL may at some point become unlawful because of the manner in which it is carried out. That's a complex issue, and I submit that it isn't one that you need to concern yourselves with for the purposes of this case because as I've explained, the Article 50 definition of "civilian" suffers from the same criticism as the one leveled to the Common Article 3 definition. And just finally, Your Honours, I'd like to make a point in follow up to Judge Schomburg's final question about whether there is a difference between civilian and civilian population and why is it that we can't see persons hors de combat once they have that status as forming part of the civilian population. And certainly in our case law, the Appeals Chamber has confirmed that the civilian population is comprised of civilians, and that comes directly from Protocol I. But what I would like to point out is a passage of the Blaskic appeals judgement, which Your Honours may consider to be interesting from the point of view of this question. And here it's -- the relevant passages are at paragraph 113 and then again following through to 115. And here the Appeals Chamber was dealing with the issue of whether the presence of non-civilians amongst a civilian population can alter the characteristic of that population. And as we know, there has been a long line of case law which has clearly established that the presence of non-civilians per se doesn't necessarily change the character. And the Blaskic Appeals Chamber was clarifying what that means. And so it dealt first of all in paragraph 113 with the presence of members of resistance groups or former combatants who've laid down their arms amongst a civilian population and expressed the view that it does not alter the characteristic of the civilian population. But compare that with the Appeals Chamber's approach to a second issue in paragraph 115 where the Chamber dealt with the presence of soldiers among the civilian population, and by soldiers we submit that the Appeals Chamber was talking about the people in our box number 4, members of the armed forces who are participating in the hostilities. And the Appeals Chamber said that it doesn't necessarily change the character of the population, but you have to look at their numbers and whether they are armed at the -- or whether they are on leave, excuse me. So you have to look at the context surrounding their presence within the population, whereas in paragraph 113 the Appeals Chamber has stated a much more unqualified proposition that the presence of hors de combat persons among the civilian population simply does not alter its characteristic. You don't have to look at how many of them are present or in what circumstances. And we submit that what the Appeals Chamber was really doing here was assimilating persons hors de combat among the civilian population in -- as suggested in Judge Schomburg's question. That concludes my submissions unless I can be of further assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you. This concludes the submissions in this appeal. Now we'll turn to Mr. Martic and ask him if he wants to address the Bench with a personal statement for not more than ten minutes as scheduled. You have the floor, Mr. Martic.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naturally. Your Honours, at the beginning of this trial in my opening statement I said that everything in the indictment against me is arbitrary and that nothing except for my first name and last name is correct and that I was not guilty under a single charge in the indictment, and I expressed hope that the Trial Chamber would establish this to be true based on the evidence led during trial. It turned out that I was deadly wrong because I was given a Trial Chamber that from the very beginning was tendentious and biassed, and their bias were based on the stereotype of Western media and their governments, and they considered us bad guys and everybody who was opposed to us good guys. In Dante's divine comedy, there is an inscription: Those who enter leave all hope behind. And this inscription is almost something that Dante wrote and that the Trial Chamber who tried me used as their guiding principle. I was tried by an inquisition, not by an impartial Tribunal. For those who are not familiar with the trial, they would have hard time to distinguish between the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber. During the trial, which lasted for over a year, Judge Moloto not a single time posed a question that could be considered as neutral, let alone favouring me. All of the questions that were put were aimed at confirming the position of the OTP. When he posed a question to Defence witness Lazar Macura, saying: Why did you not move out to Serbia yourself in 1990? You would have been recognised there as a people, and by doing so you would have made a favour both to yourselves and to Croats. And let me assure you that that same principle was advocated by greatest anti-Serb criminals such as Pavelic and Tudjman. What can be said of the Prosecution? They issued an indictment against me without any investigation 50 days after the bombing of Zagreb. They -- it was a summary-type indictment. I came here, and at the time Croatian media wrote that this indictment was equal to a parking ticket, and they pressured the Prosecution to amend the indictment. And this is when they started attributing all kinds of things to me that I have nothing to do with them. I don't envy them. They could have proclaimed me guilty of the draught that came upon Croatia because there was no rains for quite a long time. If they used the same attitude towards the Serbs, this same Prosecution which has a tonne of material of atrocious crimes against Serbs, and despite of that it did not occur to them to issue an indictment for somebody who would be responsible for crimes against Serbs. When it comes to this inquisition, it wasn't just about me. My deported Serbian people were also on trial here. History has been remodelled here. Now, I would like to turn to the political propaganda of the Western media. I will draw your attention to the conversation that I had with Mr. Cedric Thornberry, who was deputy commander of the UN peace forces in Yugoslavia. At the time, I was minister of the interior. There are minutes from that meeting on the 14th of June, 1993. This is something that my Defence used, and it was also referred to by the Trial Chamber in the judgement. The meeting with Mr. Thornberry was held about one year after the UN soldiers numbering 10.000 were deployed, including several hundred members of civilian police of the United Nations. They were deployed to the entire territory of the then-Republic of Serbian Krajina, which was split into UN protected zones. Evidence was led about it during my trial. The meeting with Mr. Thornberry was held shortly after the end of Croatian aggression against Maslenica during which Croatian forces attacked Serbian Krajina along a front that was 100 kilometres wide. About 500 Serbs were killed in that operation, dozens of villages completely destroyed, and the surviving population deported. Evidence was led about this during trial as well. I pointed out to Mr. Thornberry that we had information that Germany and France gave a go-ahead sign to Croatia to attack Krajina in the Maslenica operation, even though previously Mr. Thornberry personally assured us that Croatia would not attack us. Mr. Thornberry responded as follows, I'm quoting: "I have to say that you are completely right. They lied to us at the time, and we didn't have evidence of that." After such words, I told Mr. Thornberry that the reaction of the Security Council after this attack of Croatia against Krajina was such that instead of condemning Croatian aggression they issued statements favouring Croatia against Serbian Krajina which was the victim of aggression. I pointed out that the Western media had committed a terrible crime against Serbs because they did not inform the world of the truth, namely, that the Serbs were not an aggressor but that they were rather defending themselves. Evidence was led about this during trial too. Upon hearing these words of mine, Mr. Thornberry said as follows, and I'm quoting him verbatim: "I understand you. I understand you fully. I cannot comprehend the reports by Western media. We kept giving the truth about the refugees. It is a fact that right now the Security Council needs to have a more balanced picture. I think that the international community is also gaining a more balanced picture, and they cannot pretend that they have an impartial picture when in fact they don't. Due to political propaganda, the international community sees all Serbs in the same light. All of us here see it differently, and we tried to clarify it, but it's going very hard." As I have stated in the beginning, Your Honours, I expected that the Trial Chamber would establish the real truth, namely, that the Serbs were not aggressors but rather defended themselves in a situation when the United Nations made no attempt to protect them, even though that was their mandate. The Trial Chamber heard that only in the territory of Serbian Krajina in the area under the protection of the UN in the time-period covered by the indictment, about 7.000 Serbs were killed. Those victims are in addition to 350 victims mentioned in the indictment. Under those circumstances, the Government of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and MUP attempted to protect the entire population, regardless of ethnic or any other affiliation. The Trial Chamber has facts from the OTP expert witness Colonel Grujic, that only in operations of Croatian army which were called Flash and Storm, 300.000 Serbs were deported from Croatia in May -- from May to August 1995. In evidence, there is information from the report by Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali from 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Can I ask you to conclude your statement. Your ten minutes have expired.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that you can be tolerant enough and let me conclude. I will need several more minutes, and I've been here for several years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You have one minute maximum.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what to say, simply speaking. Before your eyes and before my eyes, there is another trial transpiring here against Croatian generals, Markac, Gotovina, and Cermak. It is a terrible thing to hear that both the Prosecution and Defence agree that that was a legitimate operation. I'm asking you, what is legitimate? Is it legitimate that the forces of UN nations under the -- and the Resolution 743 are legitimate, or is the other side legitimate? Because both of them cannot be legitimate. Croatia carried out a classic aggression: Miljevac Plateau, Maslenica, Flash, Medak pocket, and Storm. Those of that had features of genocide. There was a plan, intention, and the perpetration. Nobody, the Court, the Prosecution, paid any attention to that. Thus, unfortunately, with the aid of international community a purely fascist state of Croatia was created. This state was created on the foundations of notorious NDH which existed in World War II. Property of Serbs was seized and looted. Declaratively speaking, Croatia advocates return of Serbs, but in practice does everything to hinder that. Those who attempt to return, Croatia detains them in prisons. They issue false indictments against them about having committed war crimes against Croatian civilian population during war. I would like to remind you that the Trial Chamber treated me here as an omnipotent god who investigated some crimes but not all of them, whereas in other cases let me just say that recently 50 people who returned to their homes were killed. Do you know how many perpetrators were found? Not a single one, which means that this is something supported by the state. According to Professor Svetozar Livada this fascist state knocked down 3.200 antifascist monuments and built monuments to greatest fascist crimes, Budak, Bujanovac, and others. I will conclude shortly. The authorities of Croatia are identical to those who were in power in 1990 except for Tudjman and Susak. Stipe Mesic is the president. He used to be the president of the Presidency of the SFRY who was notorious for saying: I have concluded my task, Yugoslavia is no more. That is the same person who said that Croatia has nobody to apologise to due to World War II because they want twice: Once when they were betrayed by Axis powers, and the other time when they joined Allied forces. The main cultural content of Croatian authorities now is the concert of Marko Perkovic, Thompson, who is notorious for singing Ustasha songs and his concerts are attended by all members of the cabinet, mayor of Zagreb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Mr. Martic, I urge you to conclude. I can't allow you to abuse the proceedings. I'm sorry. Conclude. You have ten seconds to conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE APPELLANT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm concluding. Unfortunately, this current Croatia is about to enter European Union. Well, good luck, Europe. I would have a number of things to say about that entire commission and the disintegration of Yugoslavia, at which time one kind of principle was used and completely opposing principles were used for Kosovo. Gentlemen, let me tell you this, that in order to implement the interests of great powers in the territory of former Yugoslavia for the purposes of political propaganda, as Mr. Thornberry said, supported one view even though the truth was quite different. I would like to know whether your decision, as experienced Judges, would serve the truth or whether justice will be blind to serve political purposes. Should justice fail, may God help you. You have taken five minutes away from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes this appeal and the hearing. We would like to thank counsels for the parties for their submissions and all those who assisted for the conduct of the hearing, special mention and thank for our interpreters who facilitated the dialogue between the parties and the Bench. The Appeals Chamber will now rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: adjourned at 11.31 a.m.
